Institute of Competition Sciences: Plant The Moon Challenge
Integrating Meta-Analytic Insights for Martian Mycology: Growth of Pleu-
rotus Ostreatus in Regolith-Based Substrates
Gabriel Chavez1,2,3,†, Prentiss Gary1 and Gabriela Sanchez2
1California State University, Monterey Bay
2California State University, Fresno
3Arizona State University
†Principal Investigator
The authors above comprise the team known as: The Planstronauts!
Abstract
Space-based agriculture poses unique challenges due to the limited availability of nutrients, volatile moisture retention, and the sterile nature
of extraterrestrial regolith. In this study, we explored the cultivation of Pleurotus ostreatus in Martian regolith simulant (MGS-1) across different
soil and compost ratios, aiming to identify conditions conducive to mushroom mycelial growth while minimizing mold outbreaks. An automated
irrigation system (calibrated to a scaled-down water demand based on typical P. ostreatus needs) provided precise moisture control, and a
UV lighting arrangement—combined with daily pot randomization—ensured standardized environmental exposure. Over eight weeks, mold
initially outcompeted the targeted fungi in high-humidity chambers, prompting temporary drying measures and the introduction of fresh shiitake
spore plugs. Subsequent trials revealed that a sealed, humidity-rich environment facilitated robust mycelial colonization, whereas pot-based
substrates—particularly those with high regolith content—experienced slower progression. pH measurements showed that compost-rich mixes
generally stayed nearer the neutral range, whereas regolith-dominant mixes exhibited higher alkalinity. These findings highlight the importance
of substrate composition, water management, and inoculation strategies in fostering productive fungal growth and reducing invasive mold. Our
results point to a broader strategy for developing mushroom-based resource utilization, potentially enriching regolith for future plant cultivation
while offering an alternative food source.
Keywords: Extraterrestrial agriculture, Pleurotus ostreatus, Space-based farming, Plant the Moon Challenge

1. Meta Analysis
1
1.1. Abstract
2
Space-based agriculture faces unique obstacles stemming from the
3
extreme properties of extraterrestrial regolith and the operational
4
constraints of closed environments. This meta-analysis compiles and
5
synthesizes data from Plant the Moon and Plant the Mars Challenge
6
winners—educational projects in which teams grew crops in simu-
7
lated lunar or Martian soil. We surveyed the most common strategies
8
(soil amendments, microbial inoculants, water management systems)
9
that yielded successful germination, growth, and harvests, compar-
10
ing these with instances of partial or total failure. Across nearly
11
all winning experiments, participants found that regolith must be
12
enriched with nutrients, organic matter, or both to offset intrinsic
13
deficits in nitrogen, phosphorus, and organic carbon. Teams that
14
supplied additional microbes (e.g., mycorrhizae, nitrogen-fixing bac-
15
teria) saw modest gains in plant growth or root health, confirming the
16
importance of biological activity in regolith-based systems. Several
17
recurring challenges (high pH, poor water retention, salinity, and
18
incomplete composting) further align with published space agricul-
19
ture literature. Integrating these findings with peer-reviewed sources
20
reveals consensus on the necessity of multifaceted regolith ameliora-
21
tion if in situ Moon or Mars farming is to be viable. We conclude with
22
recommendations for future research, including multi-cycle com-
23
posting, robust microbial inoculation, and system-level modeling of
24
nutrient flows in regolith-based bioregenerative life support systems.
25
1.2. introduction
26
Human missions to the Moon and Mars will require reliable food
27
production systems to sustain crews during long-duration surface op-
28
erations. Unlike Earth’s soils, lunar and Martian regolith lack organic
29
matter and are chemically and structurally inhospitable to plant life
30
[3],[10],[42] [15], [40]. Lunar regolith is essentially pulverized rock
31
formed by eons of meteoritic bombardment and contains no native
32
life or readily available nutrients [34], [15]. Martian regolith has a
33
basaltic mineralogy with traces of soluble salts (e.g. perchlorates)
34
and similarly contains no organic content [22], [40]. These character-
35
istics result in an extremely nutrient-poor, sterile growing medium
36
that presents multiple challenges for plant growth: essentially zero
37
bioavailable nitrogen, limited phosphorus, micronutrients locked in
38
minerals, extreme pH, and poor water retention capacity [15], [25]. In
39
addition, potential toxins like perchlorate in Martian soil can further
40
inhibit plant development [9],[28]. Overcoming these challenges is
41
central to developing bioregenerative life support systems (BLSS) for
42
future habitats [15],[8],[19].
43
Past research in extraterrestrial agriculture has made significant
44
strides in controlled environments. NASA has successfully grown
45
Arabidopsis thaliana and other crops in small samples of actual Apollo
46
lunar regolith, demonstrating that plants can germinate and grow
47
in genuine Moon soil when provided with water and nutrients [20].
48
However, those plants showed stunted, stress-induced morphologies
49
compared to controls grown in terrestrial soil or high-quality sim-
50
ulants [20]. Similarly, multiple studies with high-fidelity regolith
51
simulants have concluded that no plant species can thrive in pure
52
simulant without nutrient supplementation [6],[18],[4]. For instance,
53
Wamelink et al. (2014) found that several crop and wild plant species
54
could germinate and survive for a time in Martian regolith simulant
55
(and to a much lesser extent in lunar simulant) using only dem-
56
ineralized water, but growth was severely limited [15]. In follow-up
57
experiments, adding organic matter from a first crop’s biomass greatly
58
improved the yield of a second planting in the simulant [15]. These
59
findings reinforce that regolith needs to be transformed into a more
60
Earth-like “soil” – via amendments and biotic inputs – to support
61
robust plant growth.

Integrating Meta-Analytic Insights for Martian Mycology: Growth of Pleurotus Ostreatus in Regolith-Based Substrates
Chavez et al.
To explore practical approaches to this problem, NASA and partner
63
organizations have engaged citizen scientists and students in exper-
64
imental challenges. The Plant the Moon Challenge and Plant the
65
Mars Challenge, run by the Institute of Competition Sciences with
66
support from NASA’s UCF Exolith Lab, provide teams with standard-
67
ized lunar or Martian soil simulant and ask them to design growth
68
experiments. Participants from middle school to college level must
69
devise ways to grow edible plants in the simulant over 8–10 weeks,
70
reporting their methods and results. These challenges have scaled
71
worldwide; by Spring 2023 over 800 teams (roughly 20,000 partici-
72
pants) were testing ideas on regolith-based cultivation [31],[29],[23].
73
Winning projects are recognized across categories such as Best Plant
74
Growth, Best Experimental Design, Innovation, and Evaluation of
75
Results. Collectively, this program has generated a trove of empirical
76
data on what works (and what fails) when attempting to “farm” the
77
Moon or Mars in a classroom setting.
78
In this study, we conduct a meta-analysis of the winning experi-
79
ments from recent Plant the Moon and Plant the Mars Challenges. By
80
synthesizing the approaches and outcomes of top-performing teams,
81
we aim to identify broad patterns of success and failure in regolith
82
agriculture. Key questions include: Which plant types tended to
83
perform well (or poorly) in simulant? Which soil amendments or
84
nutrient strategies consistently boosted growth? What growth sys-
85
tems or techniques helped mitigate issues like watering or pH? We
86
then connect these findings to the existing peer-reviewed literature
87
on space agriculture, including studies on simulant-based cultivation,
88
water use efficiency in controlled environments, the role of microbial
89
inoculants, and designs for closed-loop life support. By comparing
90
student-led trial outcomes with professional research, we can validate
91
the pedagogical experiments against scientific baselines and highlight
92
knowledge gaps. The results not only inform future challenge partic-
93
ipants but also provide insight into practical strategies for early lunar
94
or Martian greenhouses [16][34] . Ultimately, merging grassroots
95
experiments with academic research helps chart a more informed
96
path toward sustainable crop production beyond Earth.
97
1.3. Methods
98
Data Collection: We reviewed documentation of award-winning
99
projects from multiple seasons of the Plant the Moon and Plant the
100
Mars Challenge (2021 through 2024). Sources included team reports
101
(where available), abstracts from the challenge’s virtual symposia,
102
news articles, and school press releases profiling winning teams.
103
From these, we compiled information on each winning experiment’s
104
plant species, growth setup, regolith simulant type (lunar or Martian),
105
soil amendments or treatments applied, and reported outcomes (ger-
106
mination rate, plant height/biomass, any harvest attained, etc.). We
107
focused on “Best in Show” winners and category winners in Plant
108
Growth or Experimental Design, reasoning that these represented
109
the most successful or insightful approaches. In total, data on >20
110
top-ranked team projects were aggregated, spanning elementary to
111
university level teams and both lunar and Martian regolith trials.
112
Analysis: We qualitatively coded each experiment for key factors:
113
Plant Type (leafy green, root crop, legume, etc.), Amendment Strat-
114
egy (none, chemical fertilizer, organic matter, microbial inoculant,
115
Earth soil mixture, etc.), Watering and Lighting Regime, Container
116
or System (pots, hydroponic hybrid, sensors used), and Notable Chal-
117
lenges Encountered (e.g. nutrient deficiency symptoms, mold, pH
118
issues). We then identified common patterns associated with success-
119
ful plant growth (defined as achieving healthy plants or edible yields)
120
versus those associated with failed or stunted outcomes. To ensure
121
robustness, we cross-checked patterns against non-winning teams’
122
experiences reported anecdotally in articles (for example, many teams
123
that did not add nutrients observed no growth [35]). Concurrently,
124
we performed a literature review of peer-reviewed research on ex-
125
traterrestrial agriculture relevant to the observed patterns. This in-
126
cluded studies of plants grown in regolith simulants, research on
127
water use and recycling in hydroponic systems, investigations into
128
plant-microbe interactions (rhizobium, mycorrhizae) in regolith, and
129
reviews of bioregenerative life support system design. We used schol-
130
arly databases to find experimental results comparable to the chal-
131
lenge approaches (e.g. the effect of compost on simulant, or plant
132
responses to perchlorate). Each key trend from the challenge meta-
133
analysis was compared against published data for confirmation or
134
contrast. We documented whether the student-generated insights
135
aligned with scientific consensus or if any novel ideas emerged.
136
Synthesis: Finally, we synthesized the findings into a structured
137
format. We present summarized results with representative examples
138
(including a table comparing experiments) and cite literature to con-
139
textualize each point. In discussing results, we integrate the student
140
experiment outcomes with scientific explanations for the successes or
141
failures observed. All citations for challenge data refer to published
142
descriptions of the teams’ projects, while citations for external studies
143
come from academic sources. We will end our synthesis with recom-
144
mendations for Future Research that bridges both the student-led
145
experimentation and professional research needs.
146
1.4. Results
147
1.4.1. Overview of Successful vs. Unsuccessful Approaches
148
A clear overarching pattern emerged: teams that heavily amended or
149
supplemented the regolith simulant generally achieved plant growth
150
and even harvests, whereas teams that attempted to grow plants in
151
pure simulant with minimal intervention often saw failed germina-
152
tion or seedling death. The lunar and Martian simulants provided in
153
the challenge kits were, by themselves, almost incapable of support-
154
ing plant life – a finding mirrored by virtually all scientific studies
155
of these media [4]. Many participants’ final reports noted that with-
156
out added nutrients or organics, their seeds either failed to sprout
157
or produced only tiny, chlorotic (yellow) sprouts that soon stalled
158
[3],[6],[10]. An instructor whose classes trialed unamended simu-
159
lant candidly reported that the phrase “no viable sprouts” appeared
160
frequently in student research posters [35]. By contrast, nearly all
161
the award-winning teams had modified the simulant in some way
162
to improve its fertility or structure. Table 1 summarizes a selection
163
of winning experiments, illustrating the range of strategies used and
164
their outcomes.
165
1.4.2. Plant Species Performance in Regolith Simulants
166
Fast-growing, resilient crops tended to be the choices for many teams,
167
and with good reason – these species had the highest success rates.
168
Leafy greens (like collard greens, kale, lettuce) and quick-maturing
169
root vegetables (radishes especially) were repeatedly shown to ger-
170
minate and grow to harvestable size within the 2 month challenge
171
window if given appropriate care [10],[22],[16],[24],[42]. For exam-
172
ple, the Bluejay college team selected collard greens because of their
173
known hardiness and achieved significant biomass when nitrogen
174
was supplied [33],[22],[26],[42]. Nipmuc High School chose black
175
radish, a variety known for tolerating poor soils, and saw it reach
176
12cm tall in simulant with the help of inoculated nutrients[27], [45].
177
Radishes were a popular choice across many teams and consistently
178
germinated within days; their short life cycle (harvestable in 40–60
179
days) meant some teams even measured actual radish bulbs forming
180
in simulant by the end [7],[11],[24],[27],[32]. This mirrors space-
181
agriculture research where radish has been a model crop – NASA has
182
successfully grown Raphanus sativus on the International Space Sta-
183
tion in a controlled habitat [41]. The general consensus from the chal-
184
lenges and literature is that rapid-cycle, small stature plants (radishes,
185
leafy greens, herbs) are most feasible in marginal substrates because
186
they require less time and resources to reach maturity [3],[10],[25],
187
[41].
188
On the other hand, teams that attempted more resource-intensive
189
or long-season crops faced greater difficulties. A few high school
190
teams ambitiously tried to grow fruiting plants like tomatoes or pep-
191
pers in lunar simulant, but none of these made it to the winner’s

circle – typically, they failed to set fruit or even to thrive vegetatively,
193
likely due to the high nutrient demands and longer growth period re-
194
quired [5][23]. One notable success was Team YAPPERS’ cucumbers,
195
but significantly, those were grown in a 50/50 simulant-soil mixture
196
with abundant nutrients and care [44]. Pure simulant would almost
197
certainly not support a heavy-feeding fruit crop like cucumber or
198
tomato; even in the YAPPERS’ enriched conditions the mentor noted
199
the plants needed pH correction and careful feeding. Root crops like
200
potatoes were attempted by at least one winning team (the Aerospace
201
2: POTATO team). They managed to grow potato plants in lunar
202
simulant, presumably by providing substantial fertilizer (exact details
203
were proprietary), and their success suggests that even calorie-dense
204
staples can be grown if the simulant is sufficiently amended. This
205
aligns with historical experiments – for instance, Chinese scientists
206
once grew potatoes in a Mars simulant soil with added nutrients, and
207
found reasonable yields. The Purslane Gang team took a different
208
approach by choosing purslane, an edible succulent weed. Purslane
209
is extremely drought- and salt-tolerant, so it likely coped well with
210
regolith; that team won for experimental design, hinting their plant
211
did grow. In general, stress-tolerant plants (including many wild
212
species) may have a role: Wamelink et al. grew 14 wild plant species
213
in Martian simulant and found some (such as mustard and rye) could
214
grow without fertilizer better than others [15],[18].
215
A crucial point from both student experiments and research is
216
that plant choice must be matched to the growing medium’s limita-
217
tions. Crops that naturally require rich soil (e.g. most fruiting veg-
218
etables) will not do well in regolith simulant unless one essentially
219
compensates by making the medium more Earth-like via amend-
220
ments[32],[27],[13]. Crops that are adapted to poor, sandy, or alka-
221
line soils (many herbs, some legumes, certain cereals) have a better
222
chance. Interestingly, legumes (beans, peas) which could theoreti-
223
cally fix their own nitrogen were tried by a few teams (e.g. one team
224
grew lima beans). However, without the specific rhizobium bacteria
225
present, the nitrogen-fixation symbiosis would not occur, so those
226
legumes behaved like any other plant – suffering from N deficiency
227
in bare simulant. One scientific study confirms this: beans grown
228
in Mars regolith simulant without nitrogen-fixing bacteria had no
229
significant growth advantage [9],[18],[27],[34]. Thus, simply being a
230
legume is not enough; the microbial partnership must be introduced
231
(which was generally beyond the scope of most student teams except
232
where inoculants were used). In summary, fast-growing leafy and root
233
vegetables emerged as the “winners” in regolith trials, while more
234
demanding crops only succeeded when heavy amendment effectively
235
mitigated the simulant’s limitations.
236
1.4.3. Efficacy of Soil Amendments and Nutrient Strategies
237
Perhaps the strongest determinant of success in the challenges was the
238
use of soil amendments to supply nutrients and improve soil quality.
239
Virtually all winning teams employed some form of amendment,
240
falling roughly into three categories:
241
1. Chemical Fertilizers: Some teams added measured quantities
242
of mineral nutrients (e.g., nitrates, phosphates, sulfates) to the
243
simulant. The Bluejay Team explicitly compared different nitro-
244
gen fertilizers – urea, ammonium nitrate, etc. – and found all
245
three supported plant growth, whereas the no-nitrogen control
246
failed [33],[22],[26],[42]. Their data showed a dramatic contrast:
247
collard greens in nitrogen-enriched pots grew large, green leaves,
248
while those in unamended regolith were stunted and yellow [33].
249
Notably, they saw no significant growth difference between the
250
N sources, which matches agronomic knowledge that plants can
251
use nitrate, ammonium, or urea (which converts to ammonium)
252
similarly if dosage is sufficient. However, they recommended
253
urea as the optimal source because it packs the most nitrogen
254
per unit weight, an important consideration for space missions
255
where launch mass is at a premium [33]. This finding reinforces
256
a point from the literature: since lunar and Martian soils have
257
essentially zero fixed nitrogen [18],[34],[15], any productive agri-
258
culture will require an external N input, whether via fertilizer
259
or biological fixation. Other teams likely added complete hy-
260
droponic nutrient solutions to their watering regime (even if
261
not fully reported), essentially treating the simulant as an inert
262
medium while plants were fed by liquid nutrients – a strategy
263
functionally similar to hydroponics [10],[23].
264
2. Organic Matter Amendments (Compost/Soil): Organic Mat-
265
ter Amendments (Compost/Soil): A large number of successful
266
projects incorporated organic materials to “kick-start” a soil
267
ecosystem in the simulant. For example, Team YAPPERS simply
268
mixed a good quality potting soil (rich in composted organics)
269
into the simulant at a 1:1 ratio [44], [16]. This provided not
270
only nutrients (potting soil contains some fertilizer and organic
271
nitrogen) but also vastly improved the texture and water reten-
272
tion of the medium. Lunar regolith simulant on its own has
273
very poor water holding capacity (Deepagoda et al. measured it
274
as the worst among substrates tested, due to large pore spaces)
275
[15],[29],[25]. By blending in organic matter and fine particles
276
from real soil, the mixture can retain moisture much more like a
277
normal soil, preventing the rapid drying that often kills seedlings
278
in pure simulant. Other teams created their own compost: some
279
used kitchen scraps, some used manure. One high school team,
280
for instance, mixed coffee grounds and eggshells into their lunar
281
soil simulant as a homemade compost – a practice that improved
282
germination (perhaps by adding small amounts of nitrogen and
283
calcium). The efficacy of organic amendments was strongly sup-
284
ported by comparisons: an NC State University review noted
285
that mixing just 10% compost by mass into regolith simulant sig-
286
nificantly increased plant biomass in tests [15],[7],[13]. Organics
287
help pH buffering as well; lunar regolith tends to be alkaline and
288
Martian regolith slightly alkaline to neutral, but decomposition
289
products can release acids that neutralize pH or provide chelates
290
for nutrient uptake [15]. Indeed, the literature emphasizes that
291
adding organic matter (compost or manure) is a sustainable
292
way to enhance chemical fertility and biological activity in re-
293
golith, aligning with in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) goals
294
[15],[8],[19].
295
3. A few cutting-edge teams went beyond just chemistry and added
296
biology directly in the form of beneficial microbes. The Nipmuc
297
team’s use of the commercial inoculant “UltraBio” introduced
298
a consortium of soil bacteria and mycorrhizal fungi along with
299
some organic nutrient base [45],[27]. This approach recognizes
300
that on Earth, plants rely on symbiotic microbes for nutrient
301
cycling – for example, mycorrhizal fungi extend root systems
302
and help solubilize phosphorus, while nitrogen-fixing bacteria
303
can supply N to legumes [6][34]. In sterile regolith, none of
304
these helpers are present unless we add them. Nipmuc’s radish
305
growth indicated that these microbes can survive and function
306
in the simulant (since their radishes grew to a respectable size).
307
The judges praised their rigorous methodology, which likely
308
included comparing results with and without the inoculant to
309
show its benefits [45]. Peer-reviewed research backs this up:
310
preliminary studies show mycorrhizal fungi can establish in
311
lunar simulant (JSC-1A) and assist plant seeds in germinating
312
[40],[3],[18]. For instance, Trichoderma (a fungus) and Glomus
313
(a mycorrhizal fungus genus) have been shown to colonize sim-
314
ulant and improve host plant nutrient uptake [40]. Similarly,
315
rhizobium bacteria for legumes could, in theory, allow beans
316
or peas to fix nitrogen in Martian soil – one MDPI study found
317
that bean plants inoculated with Rhizobium had higher germi-
318
nation in simulant (though the effect was not huge) [9],[27],[34].
319
Overall, the challenge results and research both suggest that
320
introducing a microbial community greatly enhances regolith’s
321
capacity to support plants, essentially jump-starting the soil for-
322
mation process that is absent on lifeless moons and planets.

In contrast, teams that did not adequately amend or that misused
328
amendments often struggled. The NHTI college project is a caution-
329
ary example: they did add organic matter (composted cow manure)
330
and even attempted a “waste recycling” approach by formulating a
331
fertilizer from reclaimed nutrients (to mimic astronaut urine) [35].
332
However, their outcome was poor – likely because the amendment
333
was imbalanced. Cow manure, if not fully composted or applied in
334
excess, can lead to high salts and ammonia that inhibit seeds. Indeed,
335
the instructor speculated that the compost itself may have hindered
336
growth [35]. This underscores that not all amendments are automat-
337
ically beneficial; proper processing and dosing are critical. It also
338
reflects real-life concerns: using human wastes as fertilizer in space
339
is attractive for closure of the loop, but it must be treated to be safe
340
for plants (just as on Earth, raw manure can “burn” crops) [18],[6].
341
Another team reported that their first trial with compost failed be-
342
cause the mix became waterlogged and anaerobic (lacking drainage
343
in the simulant), leading to mold growth that killed seedlings. Thus,
344
teams learned that gradual integration of organics and maintaining
345
aeration is important – which mirrors composting best practices in
346
controlled ecological life support system (CELSS) research [15] [19].
347
In summary, the winning experiments affirm that providing nutrients
348
– whether via chemical fertilizers or organic matter – is absolutely
349
essential for plant survival in regolith [4],[10],[32]. Moreover, the
350
most effective approaches combined nutrients with improvements to
351
soil structure and biology, essentially engineering a fertile substrate
352
out of the inert simulant. These findings line up with decades of space
353
agricultural research advocating for combined physical, chemical,
354
and biological soil improvement for off-world farming [15],[13],[42].
355
The challenges demonstrate this principle in action at a small scale.
356
1.4.4. Growth System Designs and Environmental Control
357
Beyond soil chemistry, teams employed a variety of growth systems
358
and techniques to maximize their plants’ chances, and innovative
359
designs were recognized in the competition. Most teams grew their
360
plants in pots or containers under artificial lights, essentially cre-
361
ating micro-greenhouses or growth chambers in their classrooms.
362
However, within this general approach, details differed in ways that
363
affected outcomes:
364
1. Watering Methods: Teams quickly discovered that watering
365
regolith is tricky. Pure simulant, especially lunar, drains wa-
366
ter almost instantly due to large pores, leaving little moisture
367
for roots [15],[10],[28]. To combat this, successful teams used
368
frequent, small waterings or employed irrigation systems like
369
drip lines or wicks to maintain consistent moisture. The use
370
of moisture sensors (as Nipmuc did) helped avoid both drying
371
out and overwatering [45]. Some teams covered their pots with
372
plastic or grew in clear bins to reduce evaporation – effectively
373
increasing humidity around the plants. These adaptations speak
374
to the larger issue of water management in extraterrestrial farm-
375
ing: water is precious and must be efficiently used. In research
376
settings, closed-loop hydroponic systems are known to achieve
377
90% lower water usage than open soil irrigation [30] by recycling
378
nutrient solution. While most student teams did not go full hy-
379
droponic, a few flirted with the idea. For instance, one team
380
lined the bottom of their regolith pots with a hydrogel to hold
381
water, creating a crude sub-irrigation [10]. Others noted that a
382
capillary mat under the pots helped distribute water evenly. The
383
emphasis on water control in the competition results mirrors
384
NASA’s focus on water-efficient systems – NASA is even testing
385
aeroponic and hydroponic methods (the XROOTS experiment)
386
on the ISS to eliminate the need for soil at all [41].
387
2. Lighting and Temperature: All teams used artificial lighting,
388
commonly LED grow lights, to provide sufficient photosyntheti-
389
cally active radiation. Winners often optimized light intensity
390
and duration (some ran lights 16 hours a day to speed growth). A
391
few experiments compared different light colors or types, though
392
that was tangential to the soil question. Temperature was gen-
393
erally ambient (room temperature), which for many plants is
394
acceptable. A few teams growing cool-weather crops (like lettuce
395
or cabbage) made sure the room stayed 20°C. We did not find
396
cases of teams needing special temperature or CO enrichment
397
– the scale and duration were small enough that ambient CO
398
was fine, and temperature control beyond basic ranges wasn’t a
399
major reported issue. However, it is worth noting that in sealed
400
environments, plants can deplete CO and stall growth; advanced
401
life support tests on Earth (e.g., BIOS-3 in Russia) had to supple-
402
ment CO for their indoor crops. In the student projects, frequent
403
handling and open growth bins likely allowed gas exchange with
404
the room air.
405
3. Containers and Physical Structure: Most grew in small pots
406
( 10 cm diameter). A few innovative projects tried different con-
407
tainer geometries – for instance, one team used a vertical tower
408
concept (an aeroponics tower that mists roots suspended in sim-
409
ulant particles) which won an innovation award (Mars “Dust
410
to Bloom” project). Another built a terrarium with separated
411
layers of simulant and hydroponic medium, allowing roots to
412
choose. These novel systems underscore the experimental spirit:
413
some were essentially moving towards soil-less cultivation while
414
still involving regolith as a component. The judges seemed to
415
encourage such creativity, as seen with Sprayberry’s 3D-printed
416
nutrient matrix embedded in the soil [38]. By printing a lattice
417
loaded with fertilizer that sits within the simulant, they created
418
a hybrid between a soil and a controlled-release hydroponic nu-
419
trient source. This system likely ensured that as water passed
420
through the simulant, it dissolved nutrients from the printed
421
matrix, feeding the plant in a controlled way. It’s analogous to
422
putting slow-release fertilizer stakes in the soil, but tailored for
423
Martian conditions. The success of that design (winning first
424
place in Experimental Design) suggests that integrating tech-
425
nology (sensors, 3D printing, controlled delivery) with regolith
426
agriculture is a promising path.
427
4. Scale and Density Almost all teams planted relatively low den-
428
sities – often just a few seeds per pot – to avoid competition in
429
the nutrient-scarce medium. This meant yields per area were
430
low, but it maximized the chance each individual plant could

ramp up planting density for efficiency, but the results indicate

Across these system factors, a theme is that teams who treated the

moisture, adjusting pH, controlling environment) fared better than

those who treated it like a simple potted plant. The importance of

[45]. This is essentially an educational confirmation that regolith

1.4.5. Major Challenges Encountered
450
Analyzing reports of what went wrong in trials is as informative
451
as what went right. The challenges teams most frequently cited as
452
limiting plant development were:
453
1. Nutrient Deficiencies: As discussed, lack of available nu-
454
trients (especially nitrogen and phosphorus) was the number
455
one barrier. Many teams initially underestimated how barren
456
the simulant was. A few thought that because the simulant is
457
“rocky”, it might have minerals to sustain plants. They soon
458
learned that essential nutrients like N are essentially absent [15]
459
, and others like P or K, while present in the simulant’s rocks,
460
are in insoluble forms that roots cannot uptake quickly [15].
461
Visual symptoms of nutrient deficiency were common – pale
462
or reddish leaves (nitrogen or phosphorus deficiency signs) –
463
and once identified, teams corrected by adding fertilizer. The
464
literature notes that total elemental content is not the same as
465
nutrient availability; factors like pH and solubility matter [15].
466
In the simulant, any phosphorus is likely locked in apatite or
467
other minerals that dissolve too slowly. So, nutrient starvation
468
was a universal challenge requiring supplementation. (See also
469
[22],[26],[34],[42]).
470
2. pH Imbalance: Lunar regolith simulant often has a basic pH
471
(estimates range pH 9–10 for Apollo regolith; the simulant might
472
be slightly lower). Martian simulant is sometimes near neutral,
473
but depending on the batch it could be slightly alkaline from
474
basaltic salts. Several teams measured their soil pH and found
475
it outside the optimal range ( 6–7 for most crops). For instance,
476
Team YAPPERS discovered their 50/50 mix was too acidic for
477
cucumber initially (possibly the potting soil had a low pH peat
478
base) [37]. The mentor instructed them to add lime (calcium
479
carbonate) to raise the pH, after which the plants improved
480
[37]. Conversely, another team growing beans in lunar simulant
481
found the pH was too high ( pH 9) and added sulfur to lower
482
it. Managing pH was thus an important challenge – too high
483
pH can lock up nutrients like iron (causing chlorosis), too low
484
can impede nutrient uptake and harm microbes. The need for
485
pH adjustment is echoed in research: one review emphasizes
486
that pH control is vital when adding amendments to simulant
487
to ensure nutrients become bioavailable [15]. Luckily, pH is
488
one of the easier variables to correct with standard gardening
489
techniques (lime or sulfur), and winning teams did so when
490
needed. (See also [34],[42]).
491
3. Water Retention and Irrigation: Many teams struggled ini-
492
tially with how often to water. Those treating simulant like nor-
493
mal potting soil often over-watered at first (since water would
494
pool then drain quickly, giving a false impression of saturation).
495
Overwatering plus poor drainage led to temporary waterlog-
496
ging in some cases – one team mentioned algae growing on
497
the surface, indicating stagnant water. More commonly, teams
498
underwatered at first, not realizing how fast the medium dries.
499
Wilting or desiccated seedlings taught them to increase watering
500
frequency. The low water retention of simulant required teams
501
to be vigilant; automation (drip systems or frequent manual
502
checks) was almost mandatory for success. This is a known is-
503
sue: lunar soil’s porosity means it holds little water under Earth
504
gravity [15], and under lunar gravity the capillary forces might
505
behave differently (some studies suggest water might form un-
506
stable lenses in low-gravity soils). While not testable in the class-
507
room, that looming challenge was not lost on students – some
508
discussed in reports that on the Moon, watering might have to
509
be via subsurface irrigation or hydroponics to avoid water waste.
510
Indeed, NASA’s approach for lunar farming likely leans towards
511
hydroponics, partly to sidestep this tricky soil–water physics
512
problem [41]. In the competition, learning to keep the simulant
513
moist but not waterlogged was a key hurdle (and an educational
514
win in plant science for the students). (See also [10],[28],[23]).
515
4. Microbial Absence and Organic Matter Breakdown: A sub-
516
tle but important challenge was the lack of a soil ecosystem. In
517
Earth soil, countless microbes decompose organic matter, fix
518
nitrogen, and mobilize nutrients. In sterile simulant, if a team
519
added organic material, it might not break down effectively with-
520
out microbial help. Some teams who mixed in raw organics (like
521
food scraps) observed that these pieces just sat there or grew
522
mold on the surface (from airborne spores) rather than being
523
transformed into useful nutrients quickly. The Nipmuc team’s
524
success, conversely, was likely because their inoculant contained
525
decomposer microbes to process the provided organic matter.
526
The viability of microbes in the foreign regolith environment is
527
itself a challenge – pH, absence of clay/organic protective parti-
528
cles, and potential toxic metal oxides can all inhibit microbial
529
growth. Research indicates some hardy strains can survive (e.g.
530
certain Bacillus bacteria and fungi were fine in simulant tests)
531
[40], but establishing a robust microbial community may take
532
time. In a few cases, teams noted that the second half of their
533
experiment went better than the first, suspecting that “the soil
534
got conditioned.” This could be because microbial colonies fi-
535
nally established and started releasing nutrients in week 4–5,
536
improving plant growth in later weeks. It’s a reminder that time
537
is a factor – initial plantings in raw regolith might suffer, but
538
subsequent cycles (if the same soil is reused with added organic
539
inputs) could yield better results as a proto-soil ecosystem devel-
540
ops [15]. (See also [6],[27],[34],[19]).
541
5. Salinity and Toxins: While not universally encountered (be-
542
cause the simulants provided are generally low in salts), a few
543
teams did encounter issues reminiscent of Martian soil chal-
544
lenges. For example, one team that added a bit of table salt
545
to simulate Mars perchlorates ended up killing their plant –
546
illustrating the toxicity of high salinity. Martian regolith’s per-
547
chlorate content is a major concern in real missions, as even 1%
548
perchlorate can significantly stunt plant growth [9]. The student
549
challenges didn’t include actual perchlorate in the kits for safety
550
reasons, but teams discussed it in their research sections. One
551
winning team’s report involved using microorganisms to degrade
552
perchlorate in the simulant (a nod to an active area of research
553
[41]), which won an innovation award. Generally, whenever
554
a team had inexplicable plant stress, they considered whether
555
some contaminant or salt buildup was at play – for instance,
556
the NHTI team suspected high salt from their manure compost
557
[35]. Thus, salinity management emerged as a concern: teams
558
learned not to over-fertilize (which raises electrical conductivity)
559
and to flush the soil occasionally if using chemical nutrients, to
560
avoid salt accumulation. In a space greenhouse, a closed-loop

6. Dust and Particle Handling: A more operational challenge
564

In conclusion, the challenges that most frequently limited plant de-

those identified by experts for extraterrestrial agriculture: nutrient

584

585

586

1.5. Discussion
589
The aggregated results of the Plant the Moon and Plant the Mars
590
Challenge winners present a compelling, ground-level validation
591
of many principles established in formal research on space-based
592
agriculture. Broadly, the successes achieved by students reinforce
593
the idea that with sufficient amendments and control, lunar/Martian
594
regolith can serve as a growth medium for plants, albeit one that
595
starts as a blank and unforgiving slate. The failures and difficulties,
596
on the other hand, underscore the risks of treating regolith like regular
597
soil and the necessity of technological interventions to overcome its
598
shortcomings.
599
1.5.1. Nutrient supplementation is non-negotiable
600
Both the competition results and decades of research converge
601
on this point – raw regolith simply does not contain the bioavail-
602
able nutrients to support plant life beyond the seedling stage [4],
603
[15],[3],[6],[5][22],[26],[42],[36]. All winning teams added substan-
604
tial nutrients (fertilizers, compost, etc.), which was the only way to
605
get normal plant growth. This complements studies such as Caporale
606
et al. (2020), who found that Martian simulants must be enriched
607
with nutrients to sustain crops, and without supplementation even
608
hardy plants fail to thrive [4] . The Bluejay team’s finding that any
609
nitrogen source works (with growth directly proportional to added
610
N) aligns with hydroponic research where nitrogen often limits yield
611
[22][26][42]. Their recommendation of urea for efficiency is notable;
612
urea’s high N content (46%) makes it a wise choice for space transport,
613
but future work must consider that urea’s conversion to usable forms
614
depends on enzymes (urease) that might need to be present. In a
615
bioactive soil (with microbes or added enzyme), urea will break down
616
to ammonia and then to nitrate – a sequence that should occur if an
617
inoculant or even plant root exudates facilitate it [6][34]. Thus, the
618
choice of fertilizer in a BLSS context might prioritize compounds like
619
urea for weight, but also require inoculating the system with the right
620
biology to process it, or using slow-release coatings.
621
1.5.2. Organic matter and “soil” creation
622
The strong performance of teams who mixed in organic matter sup-
623
ports the concept of in-situ soil formation as advocated by NASA’s
624
bioregenerative life support researchers [15],[8],[19],[13]. By com-
625
posting organic waste (crop residues, food waste, etc.) and mixing
626
it with local regolith, future astronauts could gradually build arable
627
soil on the Moon/Mars [6][34]. The challenges showed a microcosm
628
of this: teams that added compost saw better plant vigor and water
629
retention, essentially kick-starting a soil ecosystem. Wamelink et al.
630
(2019) explicitly demonstrated that adding a first crop’s biomass to
631
lunar and Martian simulants improved the growth of a second crop
632
significantly [15], which is exactly what we see when students reuse
633
their potting mix for multiple trials – it tends to get better after the
634
“learning” crop. This is an encouraging synergy between student find-
635
ings and research: both indicate that successive planting cycles with
636
organic recycling can progressively ameliorate regolith. However, a
637
note of caution comes from cases like NHTI’s failed compost attempt
638
– showing that simply adding raw organic matter is not enough; it
639
has to be properly balanced and broken down [35]. This is where
640
controlled composting units (perhaps with temperature and aeration
641
control to produce safe, mature compost) would be vital in a space
642
habitat. The idea of composting as part of ISRU (In Situ Resource Uti-
643
lization) is increasingly discussed [15], and student experiments are
644
a great testbed for which composting techniques yield plant-friendly
645
substrate.
646
1.5.3. Microbial symbiosis and soil health
647
One of the more forward-looking aspects of some challenge projects
648
was the incorporation of microbes, reflecting an understanding that
649
plants rarely thrive alone. The success of the inoculated radish at
650
Nipmuc, for example, provides anecdotal evidence that a microbial
651
consortium can function in lunar regolith simulant [45], [27]. This
652
dovetails with recommendations in a recent npj Sustainable Agri-
653
culture review, which calls for integrating studies of plant-microbe
654
interactions in regolith-based agriculture [40]. The review noted
655
that including nitrogen-fixing bacteria and mycorrhizal fungi could
656
be game-changing for making regolith viable, as these symbioses
657
are ancient and critical for nutrient acquisition in poor soils [40],
658
[6],[18],[34]. Preliminary work cited in that review confirms that my-
659
corrhizae can colonize simulant with a suitable host plant [40]. Our
660
analysis strongly supports that notion: the presence of mycorrhizal
661
fungi in UltraBio likely aided Nipmuc’s radishes in accessing phos-
662
phorus or other micronutrients in the simulant that otherwise would
663
remain locked away. Additionally, microbes improve soil structure
664
(via biofilms and organic acids they produce) [3][19]. Looking ahead,
665
a logical next step is to simulate a true BLSS soil by having a continu-
666
ous rhizosphere in regolith – i.e., an active community of bacteria and
667
fungi around plant roots. The educational challenges have begun to
668
address this, but it could be expanded (see Recommendations). The
669
literature suggests caution in one regard: not all introduced microbes
670
will survive in the harsh regolith chemistry, and some may even pro-
671
duce harmful byproducts [27]. So, targeted selection of robust strains
672
(perhaps extremophiles) will be important. Still, the core takeaway
673
is that reinstating the biological loop (with decomposers, symbionts,
674
etc.) is critical to long-term soil fertility off-world, just as it is on Earth
675
[15],[6],[34].
676
1.5.4. Water management and system design
677
The student projects that engineered clever watering or nutrient de-
678
livery systems are essentially mirroring the path of professional space
679
food production research. For instance, the 3D nutrient matrix used
680
by Sprayberry’s team is conceptually similar to controlled-release fer-
681
tilizers used in greenhouse agriculture to ensure plants have steady
682
nutrition without daily fertigation [16],[23]. The positive result from
683
that approach indicates that “smart” fertilization techniques can re-
684
duce the need for frequent human intervention – an important factor
685
when crew time is limited. Likewise, the heavy use of moisture sen-
686
sors and automated drip irrigation by some top teams presages what
687
actual lunar/Martian greenhouses would use: you want feedback-
688
controlled irrigation to avoid drought or waterlogging [34],[42]. It

1.5.5. Comparisons of lunar vs. Martian regolith cultivation
710
Although the challenge was split into separate Moon and Mars tracks,
711
comparing across them yields insights. In general, teams working
712
with Martian simulant had a slightly easier time – many more plants
713
sprouted in MGS-1 (Mars Global Simulant) than in lunar simulant
714
JSC-1A under identical conditions, according to anecdotal reports
715
[27][18]. This aligns with findings by Wamelink et al. (2014) where
716
several species grew (albeit limitedly) in Mars simulant but almost
717
none thrived in lunar simulant without nutrients [15]. Martian sim-
718
ulant typically contains some clay and salts, which confer a bit of
719
natural structure and mineral nutrient content (for example, Mars
720
simulant has trace amounts of bio-available potassium and phospho-
721
rus) [15]. Lunar simulant, being basically pulverized volcanic glass
722
and anorthosite, has zero innate nitrogen and minimal immediately
723
available of other nutrients [15],[3],[6],[10],[22]. The student experi-
724
ments confirmed that the Moon is the tougher farming environment
725
– e.g., one team that tried the same plant in both simulants found the
726
Martian one yielded better germination. So, strategies might differ:
727
on the Moon, one might need to bring or generate more amendment
728
to get started, whereas on Mars, the soil itself gives a slight head-start
729
(tempered by the need to remove perchlorate salts). Indeed, experi-
730
ments by Oze et al. (2021) show that even 1 wt% perchlorate in Mars
731
soil stunts plants severely [9] , meaning soil washing or bioremedia-
732
tion will be necessary on Mars [14][28]. One team in the challenge
733
explicitly tackled that by proposing microbes to consume perchlorate
734
– an innovative student idea that matches ongoing NASA-funded
735
research (e.g., using perchlorate-reducing bacteria to cleanse Martian
736
soil) [39].
737

738
the systems engineering required for BLSS. Not only did they have
739
to grow a plant, they had to measure and analyze results, echoing
740
how scientists evaluate crops in life support tests. The “Best Evalua-
741
tion” awards highlight the need to quantify outcomes, which some
742
teams did via biomass measurements, soil nutrient tests, etc. This
743
is analogous to how researchers evaluate crop yield, edible biomass,
744
and resource consumption in closed tests (e.g., weighing how much
745
water was used per gram of lettuce produced in a Mars simulant study
746
[4]). The better student projects attempted to calculate things like
747
germination percentage, growth rate, and even nutritional content –
748
building skills and data that could feed into larger models [27], [29].
749
We see a strong connection here: engaging students in authentic data
750
collection adds to the collective knowledge base. NASA has leveraged
751
similar citizen science in its “Growing Beyond Earth” program for
752
selecting space crop varieties [41]. The Plant the Moon/Mars Chal-
753
lenges extend this citizen science approach to soil-based research,
754
effectively crowdsourcing preliminary trials on regolith simulants
755
across many conditions. The data from hundreds of teams, if consoli-
756
dated, could form a huge comparative dataset on what amendments/-
757
plants work best. It would be beneficial for the organizers or NASA
758
to formally analyze the combined results, as our meta-analysis only
759
sampled the highlights.

1.5.6. Implications for future extraterrestrial agriculture
761
The findings from these educational trials, buttressed by parallel sci-
762
entific evidence, point toward a hybrid approach for growing food
763
on the Moon/Mars. In the early stages of a habitat, a hydroponic or
764
soilless system might jump-start crop production because it’s more
765
predictable and can use precise nutrient solutions [41], [26], [42].
766
Over time, as missions become longer and waste materials accumu-
767
late, it would be advantageous to gradually convert some of the hydro-
768
ponic outputs (like inedible biomass, crew waste) into compost that
769
can be mixed with local regolith to create soil. This soil could then
770
support less technologically intensive crop growth (e.g., in planting
771
beds), reducing reliance on storing large volumes of nutrient solution
772
[6], [34]. The student projects demonstrate that within a couple of
773
growth cycles, regolith can begin to act more like a conventional soil
